title: 7 Keys To The First Day Of School
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin frames the first day of school as a microcosm of the entire year and lays out seven essential elements for making it count. These are: a genuine smile to activate instant likability, a peaceful pace established through calm and firm speech, a highly detailed first routine taught with excellence in mind, an engaging personal story to spark connection, an overview of the classroom management plan's rules and consequences, a focused academic lesson that shows students what real learning looks like, and a touch of fun to show that the classroom balances rigor with enjoyment. Together, he argues, these elements set a tone of trust, high expectations, and enjoyment from the very first hours. He closes with the image of a 'shrewd sea captain' who knows that a strong, well-prepared start makes for smooth sailing the rest of the year.
points: The first day of school should be treated as a microcosm representing who the teacher is and what the classroom will be all year.
A genuine smile activates instant likability and is the first step in building rapport and trust.
Teaching one common routine with excellence-level detail on day one signals that high standards apply to everything, even the mundane.
Giving an overview of the classroom management plan on day one establishes boundaries the teacher can begin enforcing immediately.
Balancing rigor with a touch of fun and humor shows students the classroom will be both demanding and enjoyable.
quotes: It’s best to think of the first day of school as a microcosm of the coming year. In other words, it should represent who you are and what you want your classroom to be.
A smile to greet your students is the first step to building rapport. It’s the first step to creating a trusting, close-knit relationship with your new class.
With your new students eager to please, early the first morning is the perfect time to send the message that you expect excellence in everything they do—even the most mundane routines.
Although you’ll use the rest of the first week to teach your classroom management plan in depth, it’s important to give an overview of your rules and consequences on the first day.
Send the message that yours is a classroom of focused, get-down-to-it learning by jumping into academics on the first day . . . but not with just any lesson.
You’ll be immediately elevated to favorite-teacher status. Your students will be excited to come back the next day and inspired to please you with their best.
